The Moral Imperative of Removal: Why Problematic Monuments Must Come Down

A Case for Systematic Reevaluation of Our Public Landscape

Note from the author: What follows is a sincere argumentative essay presenting one perspective in an ongoing democratic debate. I present the strongest version of this position because engaging seriously with ideas is more respectful than dismissing them. Readers should weigh these arguments critically alongside competing values.

Introduction

Public spaces are not neutral. Every monument erected on public land represents a collective choice—a declaration by a community about whom it venerates, whose story it tells, and whose values it enshrines in bronze and stone. When those monuments honor figures whose legacies are inextricable from systematic oppression, their continued presence constitutes an ongoing act of endorsement that a just society cannot afford. The time has come for democratic societies to undertake a thorough, systematic process of removing public statues and monuments that commemorate figures now understood to have been architects or willing instruments of racism, colonialism, and oppression. This is not the erasure of history—it is the correction of a distorted public narrative and the reclamation of shared civic space for all citizens.

I. Monuments Are Not History—They Are Arguments

The most persistent objection to monument removal is the claim that it constitutes "erasing history." This argument fundamentally misunderstands what monuments are. Monuments are not historical records. They are not primary sources. They are not educational tools. They are arguments—rhetorical assertions cast in marble and metal, making specific claims about who deserves admiration, reverence, and emulation.

Historian Karen Cox has documented extensively that the majority of Confederate monuments in the American South were not erected in the immediate aftermath of the Civil War as memorials to the dead. They were constructed decades later, during the rise of Jim Crow laws and again during the Civil Rights Movement, as deliberate assertions of white supremacist ideology. The United Daughters of the Confederacy, the organization most responsible for their proliferation, were explicit about their purpose: to construct a narrative of the "Lost Cause" that reframed a war fought to preserve slavery as a noble defense of Southern culture. These monuments were, from their inception, instruments of political intimidation.

The same pattern holds internationally. Statues of Cecil Rhodes were erected not as neutral biographical markers but as celebrations of British imperial conquest. Monuments to King Leopold II in Belgium honored a man responsible for the deaths of an estimated ten million Congolese people. Statues of Columbus across the Americas celebrate a man who initiated the transatlantic slave trade and whose own journals document horrific atrocities against Indigenous peoples.

To remove these monuments is not to erase the history of the Civil War, British colonialism, Belgian imperialism, or European exploration. That history exists—and should exist—in archives, libraries, museums, documentaries, curricula, scholarly works, and the lived memory of affected communities. Removal simply ends the celebration of the individuals who perpetrated these harms. There is a vast difference between remembering history and honoring its villains.

II. Public Space Belongs to Everyone

A statue in a public square is fundamentally different from a painting in a museum, a passage in a textbook, or an artifact in an archive. Public spaces—parks, government buildings, town squares, university campuses—belong to all members of the community. They are funded by public taxes, maintained by public resources, and experienced daily by the public at large. When a community erects a monument in such a space, it is making a statement on behalf of all its members.

Consider what it means for a Black American family to walk past a towering bronze Confederate general on their way to a courthouse where they seek justice. Consider what it means for an Indigenous student to study beneath a statue of a colonizer who advocated for the extermination of their ancestors. Consider what it means for a Congolese Belgian citizen to see Leopold II celebrated in the public squares of Brussels.

These are not abstract philosophical questions. They describe the daily lived experience of millions of people in democratic societies who are asked to move through spaces that celebrate their historical oppressors. The psychological literature on environmental microaggressions demonstrates that such symbols create measurable harm—increased stress, a diminished sense of belonging, and the reinforcement of racial hierarchies that these societies claim to have repudiated.

The philosopher Jeremy Waldron has argued persuasively that hate speech and its symbolic equivalents function as a kind of environmental pollution—they degrade the civic atmosphere for targeted groups, undermining what he calls their "assurance" that they are recognized as full and equal members of society. Public monuments to oppressors function in precisely this way. They are ambient messages of exclusion, telling certain citizens that public space was not designed with their dignity in mind.

If we accept the foundational democratic premise that public institutions and spaces must serve all citizens equally, then monuments that function as symbols of supremacy for some and symbols of subjugation for others represent a failure of that democratic commitment. Their removal is not an act of censorship but an act of inclusion.

III. Values Evolve—and Public Symbols Should Evolve With Them

Societies are not static. The moral arc of democratic civilization bends—slowly and imperfectly—toward broader recognition of human dignity. We no longer accept the divine right of kings, the legitimacy of slavery, the supposed inferiority of women, or the naturalness of racial hierarchy, even though all of these ideas were once enshrined in law and custom. Our public symbols should reflect this moral evolution.

Critics of removal often invoke a slippery slope: "If we remove Confederate statues, where does it stop? Will we tear down monuments to Washington and Jefferson?" This argument deserves a serious answer rather than dismissal.

First, the slippery slope is not the logical fallacy its critics sometimes assume. It is actually a feature of moral progress. Each generation should interrogate the symbols it has inherited and make democratic decisions about which ones still represent its values. The fact that future generations might make different choices than we do is not a reason to make no choices at all—it is the very essence of democratic self-governance.

Second, democratic deliberation is perfectly capable of drawing principled distinctions. A community might reasonably decide that a figure whose legacy includes both significant contributions and serious moral failings warrants contextual reinterpretation rather than removal—additional plaques, companion installations, renamed settings. It might decide that figures whose primary historical significance is their role in oppression—a Confederate general who fought specifically to preserve slavery, a colonial administrator whose chief accomplishment was the exploitation of colonized peoples—warrant removal entirely. The existence of difficult borderline cases does not invalidate the clear ones.

Third, and most importantly: even if we did eventually reevaluate monuments to figures like Washington and Jefferson, that would not be a catastrophe. It would be democracy working. The notion that our public landscape must remain frozen in its current form, immune to democratic revision, is itself a deeply conservative and anti-democratic position.

IV. Removal Is Restorative, Not Destructive

The language of "destruction" that often surrounds this debate is misleading. Systematic removal need not mean physical destruction. Removed monuments can be relocated to museums, where they can be presented with full historical context—not as objects of veneration but as artifacts of the ideologies that produced them. The National Museum of African American History and Culture, for instance, could powerfully house Confederate monuments as exhibits about the construction of white supremacist mythology. Budapest's Memento Park preserves communist-era statues in a dedicated outdoor museum that serves as both historical education and critical commentary. Germany's approach to Nazi-era symbols—removal from public spaces combined with extensive memorialization of victims and robust historical education—demonstrates that a society can honestly confront its past without celebrating its perpetrators.

This recontextualization actually serves historical understanding better than the current arrangement. A Confederate statue standing alone in a town square, with a brief plaque identifying the subject's name and rank, teaches almost nothing about history. The same statue in a museum, surrounded by information about when and why it was erected, who funded it, what political purposes it served, and what the person it depicts actually did, teaches a great deal. Removal from public spaces, paradoxically, enhances historical engagement rather than diminishing it.

Moreover, the spaces vacated by removed monuments create opportunities for new forms of commemoration—monuments to the enslaved people who built nations, to Indigenous communities who survived genocide, to civil rights leaders who fought for the freedoms we now celebrate. This is not erasure; it is completion. It is the telling of a fuller, more honest, more inclusive story.

V. The Social Justice Imperative

We live in a historical moment of profound reckoning. The movements for racial justice that have swept the globe—from Black Lives Matter to Indigenous rights movements to anti-colonial activism across Africa and Asia—represent an unprecedented collective demand for societies to align their professed values with their actual practices.

Monuments are not the most important dimension of this reckoning. They are less urgent than police reform, economic justice, educational equity, healthcare access, and the dismantling of structural racism in law and policy. Critics are right that monument removal alone does not constitute systemic change.

But symbols matter. They matter because they shape the stories societies tell about themselves. They matter because they signal who belongs and who doesn't. They matter because they reflect and reinforce the power structures that produce material inequality. And they matter because they are achievable—they represent a concrete, visible, democratic action that communities can take to demonstrate their commitment to justice.

The argument that we should focus on "real" issues rather than symbols creates a false dichotomy. Societies are capable of pursuing both symbolic and material change simultaneously. Indeed, the two are deeply interconnected. A society that cannot bring itself to remove a statue celebrating a slave trader is unlikely to muster the political will to address the structural legacies of the slave trade. Conversely, the democratic mobilization required to achieve monument removal builds the coalitions, political capacity, and moral clarity necessary for deeper structural change.

VI. Democratic Process, Not Mob Rule

A systematic approach to monument removal should be distinguished from spontaneous acts of toppling, though both emerge from legitimate grievance. The ideal process is democratic, deliberative, and transparent:

  1. Community review commissions composed of historians, affected community members, civil rights advocates, artists, and elected officials should evaluate existing monuments according to clear criteria.

  2. Public input processes should ensure that all community voices—especially those of historically marginalized groups most affected by the monuments in question—are heard and centered.

  3. Transparent criteria should guide decisions: What is the primary historical significance of the commemorated figure? When, why, and by whom was the monument erected? What message does the monument convey in the current civic context? Does the monument cause demonstrable harm to community members?

  4. Relocation plans should ensure that removed monuments are preserved in appropriate educational contexts rather than destroyed.

  5. Replacement processes should engage communities in imagining new forms of public commemoration that reflect shared values and inclusive histories.

This is not iconoclasm. It is civic housekeeping—the routine democratic work of ensuring that public spaces reflect the public's evolving values.

VII. Answering the Strongest Objections

"You can't judge historical figures by modern standards."

This argument assumes that no one in the past recognized the immorality of slavery, colonialism, or genocide. This is demonstrably false. Abolitionists, anti-colonial resistance leaders, and advocates for Indigenous rights existed in every era. Frederick Douglass, Bartolomé de las Casas, Olaudah Equiano, Toussaint Louverture—countless voices spoke against these systems in their own time. The figures we memorialize in bronze did not fail to meet standards that didn't exist; they chose the wrong side of moral debates that were very much alive in their own eras. Moreover, even if historical context explains their choices, it does not obligate us to celebrate those choices in perpetuity.

"This is cultural destruction akin to the Taliban or ISIS."

This comparison is both offensive and incoherent. The Taliban destroyed the Bamixa Buddhas—irreplaceable ancient artifacts belonging to a minority religious community—as an act of authoritarian religious supremacism. Democratic monument removal, by contrast, is initiated by marginalized communities through democratic processes, targets mass-produced political propaganda rather than irreplaceable ancient art, and typically involves relocation rather than destruction. Conflating the two trivializes genuine cultural destruction and delegitimizes democratic self-governance.

"Where does it end?"

It ends where democratic deliberation decides it ends. Every generation draws its own lines. The process of drawing them—debating, deliberating, deciding—is not a threat to democracy. It is democracy.

"Monuments are beautiful and contribute to the aesthetic character of cities."

Aesthetic value does not override moral considerations. Many monuments to oppressors are artistically mediocre mass productions. Those with genuine artistic merit can be preserved in museum settings. And the aesthetic argument has been deployed throughout history to defend morally indefensible things—antebellum plantations, for instance, are architecturally significant, but we do not therefore celebrate the system that built them.

Conclusion

The public landscape of every democratic society is a palimpsest—a text written and rewritten by successive generations, each adding its own layer of meaning. The monuments we have inherited were placed by communities that often held values we now rightly repudiate. To leave those monuments undisturbed is not neutrality; it is the active perpetuation of a narrative that centers oppressors and marginalizes the oppressed.

Systematic, democratic removal of monuments to figures of oppression is an act of moral clarity. It says: We remember what happened. We understand who did it. And we refuse to celebrate them for it. It makes room for new stories, new heroes, new visions of shared civic life. It creates space—literally and figuratively—for the communities that have been excluded from the narrative to see themselves reflected in the public landscape.

This is not the destruction of history. It is the beginning of a more honest, more complete, and more just relationship with it. The statues can come down. The history remains. And in the space they leave behind, we can build something that belongs to all of us.

The arguments above represent one position in a genuinely complex debate involving competing goods: inclusion, historical memory, democratic deliberation, artistic preservation, and community identity. Thoughtful people will weigh these values differently. What matters most is that the weighing happens—openly, democratically, and with the voices of those most affected at the center.
